statusValues.demoOpen: ≥1 AÇILABİLİR ders var ama SKORLANAN ders YOK — dersler açılır, hiçbiri puan vermez (her biri demoOnly/locked gerekçeli)
statusValues.comingSoon: açılabilir ders YOK; sayfası görünür, 'yakında' rozeti
statusValues.excluded: kapsam dışı; sessiz (ayrı 'neden yok' sayfası gerekmez)

statusLattice.$comment: M-F-123 aile standardı. Üçlü kafes, statü ↔ ders-durumu İKİ YÖNLÜ bağlı ve validate_content bunu kapı olarak koşuyor. Gerekçe: fazla-satmayı engelleyen disiplin EKSİK-satmayı da engellemeli — kullanıcının açabildiği ders VARSA statü onu söylemeli ('bitti = kullanıcının gördüğü yüzey' ailesi).

rule.live: style.json'da >=1 lessons[].scored == true VE honesty.measured boş değil
rule.demoOpen: style.json'da >=1 lessons[].demoOnly == true VE scored ders sayısı == 0
rule.comingSoon: style.json'da açılabilir (demoOnly) ders YOK — diskte style.json olmaması da bu duruma girer

statusLattice.openableMeans: demoOnly == true. `locked` ders AÇILAMAZ (ölçüm eksik, kilit görünür ve açılmaz), bu yüzden yalnız locked ders taşıyan bir stil demoOpen DEĞİLDİR.
statusLattice.demoOnlyFieldHasTwoMeanings: DİKKAT — bu dosyadaki stil-düzeyi `demoOnly` dizisi bir PLAN NOTU'dur ('bu stil açıldığında şu hareketler skorlanmayacak'), ders durumu DEĞİL. Kafes kararı yalnız style.json'daki gerçek lessons[] durumlarına bakar. Örnek: belly_dance/contemporary/kizomba_zouk_solo/breaking plan notu taşır ama diskte içeriği yoktur → comingSoon doğru. hip_hop_foundations ise diskte gerçek demoOnly DERS taşır → demoOpen.
statusLattice.shipGateRelationship: TASARIM GEREGI TANIMSIZ. Kafes yalnizca ICERIK gercegini soyler (acilabilir/skorlanan ders VAR MI). Ship-kapilariyla iliskisi burada TANIMLANMAZ ve yuzey-turetim katmaninda yasar (lib/app/style_availability.dart, RENDER aninda turetilir, ASLA saklanmaz). Gerekce: kafesi ship'e baglamak M-F-130'un iki-eksen-ortogonal kararini geri alir — biri digerinin vekili olur ve C-101 vekil kusuru geri doner. Sonuc: bir stil durustce hem `live` (skorlanan dersi var) hem ACILAMAZ olabilir (ship kapisi kapali); yuzey bunu KAPALI gosterir, cunku kapili seyi vaat etmek coming-soon yasaginin ters yonudur.

legalFlags.red: adlı ticari koreografi / marka adı / syllabus metni — YASAK

openDecision.question: Funk Styles paketi tek sayfa mı, dört sayfa mı?
openDecision.rationale: Blueprint Ballroom için açıkça 'TEK AİLE SAYFASI altında 7 dans' diyor; Funk Styles için 'birlikte tek genişleme' diyor — bu ship birlikteliğidir, sayfa birleşimi değil. Locking, Popping, Waacking ve Vogue ayrı adım vokabülerlerine ve ayrı köken-atıflarına sahip (Vogue: Black/Latino LGBTQ+ ballroom kültürü); tek sayfada toplamak atıf kutusunu da vokabüleri de bulanıklaştırırdı.
openDecision.pageCountEffect: 33 dalgalı sayfa + Hula (beklemede, gerekçesiyle görünür) = 34 stil sayfası; blueprint'in '~30' ifadesiyle uyumlu

demoOnly: Running Man — ayak-ucu/topuk temas zamanlaması tek-kamerada en düşük güvenli ölçüm (Tier C); 4 eğitmen ÖLÇÜLDÜ, hareket öğretilir, SKORLANMAZ (K10)
styles.note: 07-29 DÜZELTME: status 'live' idi ve YANLIŞTI — statusValues live'ı 'kursları açık, SKORLANIYOR' diye tanımlıyor, ama bu stilin skorlanan tek dersi yok (honesty.measured BOŞ: hh_bounce'ın referansı yok, Running Man Tier C, Roger Rabbit mirrorConfident:false). Eski not '≥3 bağımsız eğitmen ÖLÇÜLDÜ (C-030)' doğruydu ama ölçüm SKORLANAN derse dönüşmedi — 'ölçtüm' ile 'skorluyorum' aynı şey değil. validate_content artık bu çelişkiyi kapı olarak yakalıyor.
styles.originAttribution: Hip-hop's foundational party dances were made by Black American young people at parties, in parks and in clubs from the 1970s onward — in New York, and, for much of the groove vocabulary, in the funk scenes of California. What is taught here is social-dance vocabulary that belongs to those communities, not any one choreographer's routine.
styles.description: The party-dance foundations the rest of hip-hop is built on — a steady bounce, a rock through the chest, and the named steps that grew out of them. You dance them on the spot, to the count, before anything gets fancy.

stepGlossary.name: Bounce
stepGlossary.gloss: The steady up-and-down through the knees that most hip-hop grooves sit on.

stepGlossary.name: Rock
stepGlossary.gloss: A tilt through the chest and hips, driven from the body rather than the feet.

stepGlossary.name: Running Man
stepGlossary.gloss: Running on the spot without travelling — the feet slide back as the knee lifts.

stepGlossary.name: Roger Rabbit
stepGlossary.gloss: The Running Man's mirror image: the leg kicks back as the body leans forward.

styles.originAttribution: The fitness-class format is a late commercial packaging; the dancing inside it is not. Its steps are borrowed from Latin American social dances — salsa, merengue, cumbia, reggaeton — each with its own country and its own history, and the credit belongs to those dances rather than to the exercise format built on top of them.
styles.description: A fitness class built from Latin social-dance steps, danced for the workout rather than for a partner. You follow repeating blocks of salsa, merengue, cumbia and reggaeton footwork at a pace that keeps moving.

styles.note: Step-sheet formatı kural motoruna birebir oturuyor; yayımlı step-sheet KOPYALANMAZ, orijinal diziler
styles.originAttribution: Dancing in rows without a partner is old and widespread. The modern form draws on American country-western social dancing, which itself carries African-American and European communal dance traditions. Contemporary line dances are usually written by named choreographers and circulated as step sheets — those are their authors' work, and this app teaches its own sequences instead.
styles.description: Everybody faces the same way and dances the same sequence, no partner needed. You learn a short pattern of steps and turns, then repeat it as the dance rotates to face each wall in turn.

stepGlossary.name: Grapevine
stepGlossary.gloss: Step to the side, behind, side, then touch or turn.

stepGlossary.name: Heel dig
stepGlossary.gloss: Tapping the heel forward without taking weight.

stepGlossary.name: Kick ball change
stepGlossary.gloss: A kick, then two quick weight changes.

stepGlossary.name: Pivot turn
stepGlossary.gloss: A half turn taken on the balls of both feet.

styles.statusNote: 07-30 M-F-123 kafesi: `live` çünkü ss_l1_footwork SKORLANAN bir ders (tam-zincir, M-F-119: WRONG_FOOT + STEP_TOO_LARGE canlı, liveness testi kanıtlı) ve honesty.measured dolu. ⚠️ AÇIK GERİLİM — statü ≠ ship-hazırlığı: bpmStatus DISPUTED olduğu için validate_content hâlâ 'no lesson in this style may ship' uyarısını veriyor. Kafes DERS-DURUMUNA bakıyor (kullanıcı ship edildiğinde ne görecek), ship-kapısı AYRI bir eksen (BPM). İkisinin ilişkisi kafes tanımında YOK — koordinatöre soruldu; bu stil BPM çözülmeden yayına çıkmaz, statü live olsa da.
styles.note: Adım config'i yazıldı (ss_basic) ama HENÜZ SHIP EDİLEMEZ: BPM hâlâ çözülmedi (C-032 kapandı — hareket-üzerinden BPM çıkmaz sokaktı, ölçüldü — ama beat_annotate ile müzik-ızgarası kurucunun canlı tap'ini bekliyor, henüz koşulmadı); ss_shine_footwork referansı 4 eğitmenle KURULDU (provisional) ama ss_basic'in kendi referans takeleri (collectedTakes) hâlâ 0 — adım-config↔referans bağı ss_shine_footwork için var, ss_basic için yok. Doğrulayıcının 'diskte içerik var ama yakında' uyarısı bu yüzden BEKLENEN — içerik hazır olmakla ship edilebilir olmak aynı şey değil
styles.originAttribution: Shines are the solo passages of salsa, when partners step away from each other and dance alone. Salsa was formed by Cuban and Puerto Rican communities in New York through the 1960s and 70s, out of Cuban son and mambo and Puerto Rican traditions carried by people who had moved north. Core shines such as the Suzy Q are older still and long since public vocabulary.
styles.description: The solo footwork of salsa — the passages where partners let go and dance on their own. You work a quick-quick-slow pattern in a small space, keeping the steps tight and the count steady.

stepGlossary.name: The basic
stepGlossary.gloss: Forward and back on 1-2-3, hold on 4, then the same the other way.

stepGlossary.name: Suzy Q
stepGlossary.gloss: A travelling step where the feet twist heel-toe across each other.

stepGlossary.name: Shine footwork
stepGlossary.gloss: The solo patterns danced in place when partners let go.

styles.note: Orijinal kombolar; isimli viral koreografi öğretilmez
styles.originAttribution: Short dances made to spread on social platforms through the 2010s and 2020s. A great many of them were created by Black teenagers — often girls — whose choreography travelled worldwide while their names did not, and that pattern of uncredited borrowing is part of this form's history. This app teaches general movement vocabulary and reproduces no named creator's routine.
styles.description: Short dances made to be learned from a phone screen and danced back into one. They are built from a handful of sharp, repeatable moves timed to a specific fragment of a song.

styles.note: Ajans içeriği yüksek-dikkat; bağımsız eğitmen kanalları öncelikli. Ayna-modu zorunlu
styles.originAttribution: The 'point' is the signature hook section of a Korean pop song's choreography, a convention of the Korean idol industry that grew from the 1990s onward. These routines are the work of named choreographers and production companies. They are not reproduced here; what can be taught is the movement vocabulary they draw on.
styles.description: The signature hook section of a Korean pop routine — the part everyone recognises and copies. It is dense, precise and short, and it rewards clean shapes over big movement.

styles.note: Yalnız 2 kanal bulundu — ek tarama görevi
styles.originAttribution: Bachata comes from the Dominican Republic, growing out of guitar music of the mid-twentieth century that was for decades dismissed as rural and disreputable by the country's elite before it became a national music and then a social dance danced worldwide.
styles.description: Bachata danced on your own: a four-step pattern side to side, with a tap or a hip on the fourth. The feel lives in the knees and hips rather than in how far you travel.

stepGlossary.name: Side basic
stepGlossary.gloss: Three steps to the side and a tap or hip on the fourth.

stepGlossary.name: Forward basic
stepGlossary.gloss: The same four counts taken forward and back.

stepGlossary.name: Hip motion
stepGlossary.gloss: The hip lift on the fourth count that gives bachata its shape.

styles.note: Amapiano döner trend-paketi: sabit müfredat değil, viral döngü. Köken-atıf kutusu zorunlu
styles.originAttribution: Afrobeats is a West African popular music movement centred on Nigeria and Ghana from the 2000s, and its dances — azonto, shaku shaku, zanku and others — each came out of particular urban scenes and particular dancers. It is a different thing from Fela Kuti's Afrobeat, and the two are often confused.
styles.description: The dances of West African pop — a family of named steps that arrive with the songs and spread fast. Most are led from the legs and shoulders, danced light and loose on the spot.

stepGlossary.name: Azonto
stepGlossary.gloss: A Ghanaian step built on bent knees and mimed hand gestures.

stepGlossary.name: Shaku shaku
stepGlossary.gloss: Crossed hands at the forehead over a light, skipping leg.

stepGlossary.name: Zanku / legwork
stepGlossary.gloss: Fast, loose lower-leg movement danced on the spot.

stepGlossary.name: Gwara gwara
stepGlossary.gloss: A leg sweep and lean, from South African house dancing.

styles.originAttribution: Jamaican dancehall grew out of Kingston's sound-system culture from the late 1970s. Unusually among popular dances, its steps are individually named and datable, and most can be traced to a specific dancer and a specific moment — which makes crediting them possible in a way it often is not elsewhere.
styles.description: Jamaican dancehall is a vocabulary of named steps, each with its own attitude and its own moment. You learn them one at a time and then choose between them as the riddim moves.

styles.note: ≥60fps önerisi — hızlı ayak işi
styles.originAttribution: The shuffle developed in Melbourne's rave and underground club scene from the late 1980s and 1990s, and later picked up related 'cutting shapes' variants from UK dance scenes. It is a club dance made by dancers on floors, with no single author.
styles.description: A fast shuffling footwork danced to four-on-the-floor electronic music. The whole dance lives below the knees — the upper body stays quiet while the feet slide and kick.

styles.originAttribution: 'Belly dance' is an outsider's name. The dances it points at — raqs sharqi and raqs baladi in Arabic, oryantal dans in Turkish, and related regional forms — belong to Egypt, the Levant, Turkey and the wider region, and lived in family and community celebration long before any staged or exported version of them.
styles.description: A dance of the hips, ribs and spine, where the movement is isolated rather than travelled. You learn to move one part of the body while the rest stays still, which is harder and better than it sounds.

stepGlossary.name: Hip drop
stepGlossary.gloss: An accented drop of one hip, isolated from the rest of the body.

stepGlossary.name: Shimmy
stepGlossary.gloss: A fast shiver of the hips or shoulders, driven from the legs.

stepGlossary.name: Undulation
stepGlossary.gloss: A rolling wave through the chest, belly and hips.

stepGlossary.name: Figure eight
stepGlossary.gloss: The hips tracing a horizontal or vertical eight.

styles.note: Mudra: el-landmark varsa skorlu, yoksa demo
styles.originAttribution: Film dance from the Hindi-language film industry in Mumbai, which from the mid-twentieth century blended Indian classical forms such as kathak and bharatanatyam with folk traditions including bhangra and garba, and with Western popular dance. Individual film routines are their choreographers' work and are not reproduced here.
styles.description: Film dance from Hindi cinema — expressive, rhythmic and unafraid of scale. It borrows from Indian classical and folk forms and from Western popular dance, often within a single song.

styles.note: Bachata/shines deseninin birebir tekrarı — en ucuz ekleme
styles.originAttribution: Merengue is the national dance of the Dominican Republic, danced there long before it was promoted abroad, and it carries the same African and European meeting that shaped the island's music.
styles.description: A simple, insistent march danced on the spot or side to side, with the hips carrying what the feet keep plain. It is the most quickly learned of the Latin social dances and the hardest to make look good.

styles.originAttribution: Cumbia began on Colombia's Caribbean coast, in the meeting of Indigenous, African and Spanish traditions, and then travelled: Mexico, Argentina, Peru and others each grew their own cumbia with its own step and its own feel. Naming it one dance understates it.
styles.description: A dragging, unhurried step danced with one foot brushing the floor, in a small circle or a shuffle. Every country that took up cumbia bent it a different way, so the feel varies more than the footwork.

styles.note: TEK sayfa, 7 sekme. ISTD/WDSF Bronze→Gold yapısı ESİNLENİLİR; syllabus METNİ telifli, anlatım ORİJİNAL
styles.originAttribution: The competitive 'Latin' syllabus was standardised in Britain in the early twentieth century out of dances that were not British: cha-cha and rumba from Cuba, samba from Brazil, jive from African-American swing, paso doble from Spanish sources. The codification is a real craft with its own history; it is not the origin of the dances, and the published syllabus texts belong to the bodies that wrote them.
styles.description: The technique behind the competitive Latin dances, practised without a partner. You drill weight, turnout, hip action and foot pressure — the parts that are yours to control whoever you are dancing with.

stepGlossary.name: Cucaracha
stepGlossary.gloss: A side step that presses into the floor without travelling.

stepGlossary.name: Spot turn
stepGlossary.gloss: A turn taken on the spot, one foot crossing in front.

stepGlossary.name: New York
stepGlossary.gloss: A checked step to the side with the arms opening in opposition.

stepGlossary.name: Hip action
stepGlossary.gloss: The settling of the hip that follows a straightened knee.

styles.note: PERKÜSİF ONSET: shuffle/flap/stamp ayrımı + zamanlama (K9). ISTD 6-seviye esinli
styles.originAttribution: Tap was made in the United States, largely by Black American dancers, out of the meeting of African rhythmic dance with Irish and English step dancing — a meeting that happened under slavery and segregation, in circumstances its dancers did not choose. Its history is inseparable from that.
styles.description: Dancing that is also drumming: the shoes make the sound and the sound is the point. You learn to break a step into its separate hits and to place each one where you meant it.

stepGlossary.name: Shuffle
stepGlossary.gloss: Two sounds from one foot: brush out, brush back.

stepGlossary.name: Flap
stepGlossary.gloss: Brush forward and step down — two sounds, weight transferred.

stepGlossary.name: Ball change
stepGlossary.gloss: A quick weight change between the ball of one foot and the other.

stepGlossary.name: Time step
stepGlossary.gloss: A repeating rhythmic phrase used to set tempo and trade with musicians.

styles.originAttribution: Locking was created by Don Campbell in Los Angeles around 1970 — one of the rare street dances whose invention is attributed to a single named dancer, and it was originally called Campbellocking after him. It spread through his group and through television.
styles.description: A funk style built on stopping — you move fast, freeze hard, and hold the pause a beat longer than feels comfortable. The freeze is the punchline and the timing is the joke.

stepGlossary.name: Lock
stepGlossary.gloss: The sudden stop that names the dance — arrive and hold.

stepGlossary.name: Point
stepGlossary.gloss: An extended arm and finger, usually straight out of a lock.

stepGlossary.name: Wrist roll
stepGlossary.gloss: A circling of the hands that carries you between locks.

stepGlossary.name: Scoobot
stepGlossary.gloss: A travelling step with a kick and a hop, danced side to side.

styles.note: Hit'ler RhythmEngine'e birebir uyum
styles.originAttribution: Popping came out of the funk scenes of Fresno and Los Angeles in the 1970s, with Boogaloo Sam and the Electric Boogaloos central to its development and its spread. The related boogaloo and related Californian funk styles are distinct dances, often flattened together by outsiders.
styles.description: A funk style built on the pop: a sharp contraction of a muscle that snaps the body on the beat. Around it sit smoother illusions — waves, glides and robotics — that make the hits land harder.

stepGlossary.name: Pop / hit
stepGlossary.gloss: A sharp muscle contraction that snaps the body on the beat.

stepGlossary.name: Wave
stepGlossary.gloss: An impulse passed through the arms or body so it reads as travelling.

stepGlossary.name: Glide
stepGlossary.gloss: Footwork that makes you look like you are sliding rather than stepping.

stepGlossary.name: Robot
stepGlossary.gloss: Movement broken into separate mechanical segments, with pauses between.

styles.originAttribution: Waacking was created in Black and Latino LGBTQ+ clubs in Los Angeles in the 1970s, danced to disco, by people who in many cases could not be publicly out anywhere else. It is a dance that came from a refuge, and a number of its originators were lost to the AIDS epidemic before it was widely credited.
styles.description: Fast arm work danced to disco, all whips, circles and stops, with the poses between them doing as much as the movement. It is a dance about presence as much as speed.

stepGlossary.name: Whack / arm swing
stepGlossary.gloss: A fast circular arm strike that stops dead on the beat.

stepGlossary.name: Pose
stepGlossary.gloss: The held shape between the arm work — half the dance lives here.

stepGlossary.name: Spin
stepGlossary.gloss: A turn used to change facing and reset the arms.

styles.originAttribution: Vogue comes from the ballroom scene built by Black and Latino LGBTQ+ communities in Harlem and across New York, where houses formed as chosen families and competed at balls. It was a culture of survival long before it was a style anyone outside it borrowed, and the borrowing has usually been done without credit or return.
styles.description: Movement built out of poses — lines, angles and hands, danced with the confidence the ballroom scene demands. Its elements are named and judged, and each one asks for something different from you.

stepGlossary.name: Hands performance
stepGlossary.gloss: Storytelling with the hands and arms, close to the face and body.

stepGlossary.name: Catwalk
stepGlossary.gloss: A walk with the hips and shoulders swinging against each other.

stepGlossary.name: Duckwalk
stepGlossary.gloss: Travelling low in a squat, kicking one foot forward at a time.

stepGlossary.name: Floor performance
stepGlossary.gloss: Work taken down to the ground without losing line or control.

stepGlossary.name: Spins and dips
stepGlossary.gloss: A turn that drops into a controlled fall onto the back leg.

styles.originAttribution: Jazz dance grew out of African-American vernacular dance alongside jazz music from the early twentieth century, in social halls before theatres. The studio and stage forms taught today are descendants of that social dancing, and often carry its steps under other names.
styles.description: The studio descendant of African-American social dance: isolations, sharp lines, and steps that travel with attitude. It sits underneath most commercial and musical-theatre dancing you have seen.

stepGlossary.name: Jazz square
stepGlossary.gloss: Four steps tracing a box: cross, back, side, forward.

stepGlossary.name: Pas de bourrée
stepGlossary.gloss: Three quick steps that change your weight and facing.

stepGlossary.name: Chassé
stepGlossary.gloss: A travelling step where one foot chases the other.

stepGlossary.name: Isolation
stepGlossary.gloss: Moving one body part while the rest stays still.

styles.note: Karnaval solo samba. Gafieira ayrı SKU DEĞİL — ileri-stil katmanı
styles.originAttribution: Samba no pé is the solo footwork of Brazilian samba, an Afro-Brazilian form that grew in the communities of Bahia and Rio de Janeiro and is carried today by the samba schools and their carnival. The dance and the drumming are one tradition, not two.
styles.description: The solo footwork of Brazilian samba — a bouncing three-step danced in the time of two, fast and low. The bounce comes from the knees, not from jumping.

styles.note: Shim Sham = sabit 32-count rutin → DTW-dostu
styles.originAttribution: Solo jazz and the Charleston are African-American social dances of the 1920s and 30s, danced in Harlem and far beyond it, and named in the Charleston's case for the South Carolina city. They were popular dances of their moment before they were anybody's heritage style.
styles.description: The social dances of the 1920s and 30s, danced alone: swinging kicks, bouncy footwork and named steps with names as good as the steps. It is dance built for a live band and it still feels like it.

stepGlossary.name: Charleston
stepGlossary.gloss: Rock back and kick forward, swinging from the hips.

stepGlossary.name: Suzie Q
stepGlossary.gloss: Travelling sideways with the feet twisting heel-toe.

stepGlossary.name: Boogie back
stepGlossary.gloss: Travelling backwards with a bouncing shuffle.

stepGlossary.name: Shorty George
stepGlossary.gloss: Walking forward low, knees together, pointing at the floor.

styles.note: Dhol ritmi RhythmEngine'e uygun; müfredat ORİJİNAL geliştirilir
styles.originAttribution: Bhangra is a harvest dance of the Punjab, the region now divided between India and Pakistan, tied to Baisakhi and to the farming year. It has a second life as a British-Punjabi popular music and club form from the 1980s, made by the children of migrants — both are real bhangra and they are not the same dance.
styles.description: A high-energy Punjabi dance of raised arms, bouncing shoulders and stamping feet, danced to the dhol drum. It is meant to be big — the small version does not work.

styles.note: Ev-desteği modu (sandalye/tezgâh)
styles.originAttribution: Ballet was codified in the Italian and then French courts, which is why its vocabulary is French, and later developed further in Russia, Denmark and elsewhere. Barre work is its daily training practice rather than a dance in itself.
styles.description: The daily training practice of ballet, done holding a barre. You work through a fixed order of exercises that build turnout, control and line before anything travels across a floor.

stepGlossary.name: Plié
stepGlossary.gloss: A bend of the knees over the toes, the basis of every jump and landing.

stepGlossary.name: Tendu
stepGlossary.gloss: A stretch of the foot along the floor until only the toe touches.

stepGlossary.name: Dégagé
stepGlossary.gloss: A tendu that keeps going until the foot leaves the floor.

stepGlossary.name: Rond de jambe
stepGlossary.gloss: A circling of the leg, on the floor or in the air.

stepGlossary.name: Relevé
stepGlossary.gloss: A rise onto the balls of the feet.

styles.originAttribution: Contemporary dance descends from the modern dance of the early twentieth century, made by choreographers — many of them women — who deliberately refused ballet's codified vocabulary and built their own. It is less a single technique than a family of them, each with a named lineage.
styles.description: A family of techniques descended from twentieth-century modern dance, built on weight, breath and release rather than on a fixed vocabulary. Floorwork and falling are technique here, not accidents.

styles.note: Zapateado = onset skorlama; palmas bonus
styles.originAttribution: Flamenco was formed in Andalusia, in southern Spain, with Romani (Gitano) communities at its centre, alongside Andalusian, Moorish and Jewish influences, and it grew among people who were persecuted there. Cante, guitar and dance are one art; teaching the dance alone is already a simplification.
styles.description: Percussive footwork, carriage and hand work, danced to guitar and song. The dance answers the music rather than decorating it, which is why the counting matters more than the steps at first.

stepGlossary.name: Zapateado
stepGlossary.gloss: The percussive footwork — heel, toe and sole, each its own sound.

stepGlossary.name: Braceo
stepGlossary.gloss: The carriage and circling of the arms.

stepGlossary.name: Marcaje
stepGlossary.gloss: Marking time with the body while the song takes the foreground.

stepGlossary.name: Remate
stepGlossary.gloss: A short ending flourish that closes a phrase.

styles.note: Hard-shoe = onset; soft-shoe = poz+sıçrama kadraj kalibrasyonu. TEK lineage seçilir
styles.originAttribution: Irish dance covers both the social forms — céilí and set dancing, danced together — and the competitive step dance most familiar abroad. Its transmission survived long periods when Irish cultural practice was suppressed, and the modern competitive form was shaped substantially in the twentieth century.
styles.description: Sharp, quick footwork with the upper body held still, danced on the balls of the feet. The legs do everything and they do it in a very small amount of space.

demoOnly: cambré — skor baskısı YOK, güvenlik çerçevesi
styles.originAttribution: Kizomba came from Angola, growing out of semba, and took shape alongside Cape Verdean and French Antillean zouk music. It is an African dance with a specific history, frequently marketed abroad as though it were generically 'Latin'.
styles.description: A slow, grounded walking dance from Angola, practised here on your own. The step is simple and the difficulty is all in the weight — where it sits and how long it takes to arrive.

styles.note: YALNIZ solo footwork + tef/el çırpma tekniği. Dandiya-Raas kapsam DIŞI (çift-sopa, solo öğrenilemez)
styles.originAttribution: Garba is a devotional circle dance of Gujarat, in western India, danced during Navratri in honour of the goddess. It is worship as much as it is dance, and the circle around the lamp or image is the point of the form rather than a staging choice.
styles.description: A circle dance for Navratri, built on clapping patterns and a turning step that carries you around the centre. It is danced for hours, so it starts gently and it is meant to.

stepGlossary.name: Do taali
stepGlossary.gloss: The two-clap step — the pattern most garba starts from.

stepGlossary.name: Tran taali
stepGlossary.gloss: The three-clap step, faster and with a turn.

stepGlossary.name: Circle step
stepGlossary.gloss: The travelling step that carries the whole circle around the centre.

styles.note: 3/4 kamera açısı modu. Store-policy turu bu kovaya BİRLİKTE bakar — W4 öncesi kurucu onayı
styles.originAttribution: Twerk's immediate lineage runs through New Orleans bounce, and behind that through West and Central African dances in which isolated hip and glute movement is long-established technique. Reggaeton grew from Panama and Puerto Rico out of reggae en español and dancehall. Both were treated as vulgar while they belonged to Black and Latino communities and as fashionable once they did not.
styles.description: Isolated hip and glute movement danced to reggaeton and its relatives — technique that is far older and far more controlled than its reputation. The control comes from the lower back and the legs.

styles.originAttribution: Heels is a studio style rather than a community dance — it took shape in commercial dance studios, largely in Los Angeles, drawing on jazz, on waacking and on burlesque and cabaret traditions. Much of what gives it its character was carried in by queer dancers from those older forms.
styles.description: A studio style danced in heels, drawing on jazz, waacking and cabaret. Standing, walking and turning all change in heels, so the first work is not choreography but balance.

styles.note: Toprock/uprock SKORLU
styles.originAttribution: Breaking was created by Black and Puerto Rican young people in the Bronx in the early 1970s, as part of the same emerging hip-hop culture as DJing, MCing and writing. Its crews and its named moves have documented originators, and the dance existed for decades before institutions took an interest in it.
styles.description: Danced upright and on the floor: you start on your feet, drop, work through footwork, and finish on a freeze. It is the most athletic dance here and the one with the clearest structure.

stepGlossary.name: Toprock
stepGlossary.gloss: The upright dancing you open with, before going down to the floor.

stepGlossary.name: Go-down
stepGlossary.gloss: The transition that takes you from standing into floorwork.

stepGlossary.name: Footwork
stepGlossary.gloss: Steps danced on hands and feet, circling around your own centre.

stepGlossary.name: Freeze
stepGlossary.gloss: A held shape, usually balanced on hands, that stops the phrase.

stepGlossary.name: Power move
stepGlossary.gloss: Continuous spinning momentum — the acrobatic end of the dance.

styles.onHoldReason: Yaşayan kültürel-manevi pratik. hālau/kumu-hula ORTAKLIĞI olmadan yapılmaz; jenerik kaynakla içerik üretimi YASAK. Sayfada bu gerekçe açıkça yazılır.
styles.originAttribution: Hula is a Native Hawaiian practice in which dance, chant (mele), genealogy and spiritual life are one thing. It is taught within a hālau under a kumu hula, and that relationship is the form — not an optional traditional framing around it. Hula was suppressed and nearly severed under missionary and colonial rule, and its survival is the direct result of people who kept teaching it anyway.
